mark_split.label: Divide, then set up the form

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.67 — SAQ chapter 11 Partial Fractions, answer 102. Printed appearances: TS 16, 22. ⚠ THE 1+1+1+1 SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — this chapter prints no [N Marks] tags against any answer, only tick boxes. The split is the four moves of the method (set up the form · clear the denominators · find the constants · write the result), one mark each, and the SAME split and the SAME step ids (s1_form, s2_identity, s3_constants, s4_result) are used on all fifteen cards of this unit, deliberately: they are one method over different fractions. For the improper fractions the division lives inside s1_form, and for the (x − 3)³ question the substitution x − 3 = y takes the place of the form. The book's SAQ chapter header carries ★★★ and reads '4 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-2A Section B runs Q11–Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q15 is the Partial Fractions slot (the chapter has no Section A or Section C slot). Model Paper 4 (book p.117) asks exactly this question at Q15. No two-book check and no board back-test exist for this paper — recorded, not hidden. A back-test against the book's own six papers (the five Model Guess Papers plus the Bullet Model Paper, 199 slot-instances) WAS run on 2026-08-29: all 199 resolved to an authored card, and every one carried the section and marks its slot implies. That is a substitute corpus, not a board paper — it cannot show what the board asks that this book omits. The book shows the long division in a boxed layout; the card writes the same three subtraction rows as three lines and states the product-plus-remainder identity, which a student can check by expanding. Truth check: expanding (x² − 3x + 2)(x² + 3x + 7) gives x⁴ − 15x + 14, so x⁴ = (x² − 3x + 2)(x² + 3x + 7) + 15x − 14; and putting x = 0 in the remainder identity gives −14 = A(−2) + B(−1) = 2 − 16 = −14 with A = −1, B = 16.

recall_prompt: Say how you would resolve x⁴/((x − 1)(x − 2)) into partial fractions — name each move in order, starting with what must be done before the form is written.
insider_note: The division must run until the remainder degree drops below 2 — quotient x² + 3x + 7, remainder 15x − 14 — and that quotient returns in the final answer; stopping the division early makes every later constant wrong.

steps.label: Divide, then set up the form
steps.margin_note: First mark. Degree 4 over degree 2: improper. Divide x⁴ by x² − 3x + 2 in three rows: take away x² times, then 3x times, then 7 times. Quotient x² + 3x + 7, remainder 15x − 14.
steps.memory_tip: Divide until the remainder's degree drops BELOW 2: three rows give quotient x² + 3x + 7, remainder 15x − 14.

recall.must_convey: That the fraction is improper, x⁴ divided by x² − 3x + 2 gives quotient x² + 3x + 7 and remainder 15x − 14, and only (15x − 14)/((x − 1)(x − 2)) is written as A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 2).

heard_as: x squared plus three x plus seven

steps.why: A fraction with the higher degree on top is not a sum of fractions over the factors; it is a polynomial plus such a sum. The division finds the polynomial x² + 3x + 7, and the remainder over the same denominator is proper.
common_mistakes: Writing A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 2) for x⁴ itself without dividing.
Stopping the division after one or two rows and taking 7x² − 6x as the remainder; the degree of the remainder must be less than 2.
A sign error in 7x² − 6x − 7x² + 21x − 14 = 15x − 14, giving −6x + 21x wrongly as 27x.

steps.label: Clear the denominators
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Multiply the remainder fraction equation by (x − 1)(x − 2). The quotient stays aside.
steps.memory_tip: The identity is on the remainder 15x − 14, not on x⁴. The quotient stays aside.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying the remainder equation through gives 15x − 14 = A(x − 2) + B(x − 1).
accept: multiply both sides by x minus one into x minus two to get fifteen x minus fourteen equals A into x minus two plus B into x minus one

steps.why: The identity belongs to the proper fraction, so its left side is the remainder 15x − 14. Writing x⁴ there makes every later line wrong.
common_mistakes: Carrying the quotient into the identity.

steps.label: Find the constants
steps.margin_note: Third mark. x = 1 gives 1 = −A so A = −1. x = 2 gives 16 = B. Two roots, two constants.
steps.memory_tip: Substitute into 15x − 14: x = 1 gives 1 = −A, and x = 2 gives 16 = B.

recall.must_convey: That x = 1 gives A = −1 and x = 2 gives B = 16.

steps.why: Each root of a linear factor makes the other term zero and leaves one constant multiplied by a known number. The constants follow directly; no coefficient comparison is needed here.
common_mistakes: Putting x = 1 and writing A(1 − 2) = A instead of −A, giving A = 1.
Putting x = 1 into x⁴ instead of into 15x − 14.

steps.label: Write the result
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The quotient x² + 3x + 7 comes first, then −1/(x − 1) + 16/(x − 2). Write the original fraction on the left.
steps.memory_tip: The quotient x² + 3x + 7 comes first, then −1/(x − 1) + 16/(x − 2). Check x = 0: −14 = 2 − 16.

recall.must_convey: That the fraction equals x² + 3x + 7 − 1/(x − 1) + 16/(x − 2), with the quotient in front.

steps.why: The quotient is part of the answer; without it the line resolves only the remainder fraction. The examiner looks for the polynomial and both fractions with their signs.
common_mistakes: Forgetting x² + 3x + 7 in the final line.
